endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: Inclusive design extends beyond outcome auditing: PH-LLMs should support languages prevalent in target populations, incorporate cultural adaptation beyond direct translation, conform to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 [ 129 ], and provide health-literacy adaptation through adjustable response complexity and optional comprehension checks [ 96 , 130 ].

evidence.title: ALERT-ED: Awareness and Linkage to Resources for At-Risk Emergency Department Patients: Interviews with Older Patients, Caregivers, and Nurses
evidence.venue: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
evidence.outcome: Accessibility of patient-facing fall-risk chatbot for users with impairments, per interview themes
evidence.effect: Interview thematic analysis identified remaining accessibility gaps for users with impairments (theme 7), although usability was otherwise rated high because of the QR interface.
evidence.quote: Interviews of 6 nurses, 12 patients, and 4 caregivers revealed seven themes: (1) feasibility depends on dissemination strategies and workflow alignment; (2) barriers include limited awareness and nursing time constraints; (3) acceptability improves trust, readability, and personalization; (4) expanding scope to enhance engagement; (5) privacy and artificial intelligence skepticism persist; (6) usability is high due to the QR interface; and (7) accessibility gaps remain for users with impairments.

evidence.effect: WCAG 2.2 AA text criteria passed; interface requirements moved from 14/27/18 to 38/14/7 (MET/PARTIAL/UNMET).
evidence.quote: Interface requirements moved from 14/27/18 to 38/14/7 (MET/PARTIAL/UNMET); Nielsen severity resolved 7 of 10 issues; WCAG 2.2 AA text criteria passed.

commentary.bottom_line: One offline automated benchmark found that an AI interface passed WCAG 2.2 AA text criteria and that its met requirements rose from 14 to 38 after revision, but no study has tested whether pre-deployment accessibility verification changes access or outcomes for patients with disabilities. Two deployed chatbots received high usability ratings while still showing accessibility gaps, which suggests that satisfaction scores alone may not detect the problem.

perspectives.view: A single level 5 automated benchmark in a simulated setting tests the practice, and it measures interface conformance rather than patient outcomes. Certainty is very low because of indirectness, the absence of real users with disabilities, no comparison group, and no replication. The two hazard studies show that gaps exist but do not test verification itself.

One deployed tool used 10-px text and a 2.56:1 contrast ratio while averaging a SUS near 92. Another fall-risk chatbot rated highly for usability still left gaps for users with impairments. These findings suggest that inaccessible features can pass routine user acceptance checks and reach patients unless someone measures them against a standard.

The benchmark shows that automated conformance checks can be run and repeated during development, with unmet requirements falling from 18 to 7. The study does not report the staff time, tooling, or manual review required, and automated checks covered text criteria only. How well this process fits a health system's procurement workflow remains untested.

The only study testing verification did not report enrolling limited English proficiency, Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. The fall-risk chatbot study included limited English proficiency patients and older adults and found remaining accessibility gaps, which indicates that the populations at greatest risk of exclusion are absent from the test of the safeguard.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks deployers to confirm adherence to accessibility standards, and one commentary names WCAG 2.2 as the reference. These endorsements rest on expert consensus. The benchmark used WCAG 2.2 AA as its measure, which suggests that this standard can serve as a practical verification target, though no study links conformance to patient benefit.

Patients in the fall-risk chatbot study described accessibility gaps even though they found the QR interface easy to use. For patients with visual or motor impairments, a tool that others rate as usable may still be one they cannot operate. The evidence does not show whether verification restores their access or their path to a human.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared AI tools that underwent pre-deployment accessibility verification with tools that did not, using outcomes such as task completion, error rates, or abandonment among patients with visual, motor, cognitive, or hearing impairments in real deployments. Studies should also measure how much automated checks miss relative to manual testing with disabled users, and what verification costs a health system.
commentary.underserved_note: The single study that tested the practice did not report including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study included limited English proficiency patients and older adults and found accessibility gaps, so the populations most likely to be excluded are documented as affected but are not represented in any test of whether verification helps them.
